summary: Two NVIDIA authors evolve the natural-language skill file injected into a Claude Opus 4.6 Verilog agent. A GPT-5 oracle mines rollout traces, Claude Sonnet 4.5 mutates the skill, and selection is driven by a hidden-verifier-led score, with an optional budgeted 'dense' verifier feedback tool. On 8 CVDP tasks the seed agent failed, the full configuration achieves at least one pass on 6/8 tasks after 640 rollouts per configuration.

claims.claim: Trace2Skill with dense verifier feedback solves 6/8 hard tasks (33.6% pass rate) versus 0/8 for the seed agent.
claims.evidence: Table 3: C1 0/8 with 32 rollouts; C4 6/8, 33.6%, with 640 rollouts. 'Solved' means at least one pass across 80 rollouts per task (e.g., PCIe 1/80, §4.4), so this is closer to pass@80 versus pass@4. Compute is 20x unequal, and there is no held-out evaluation: skills are optimized and scored on the same 8 tasks (§3.1).

claims.claim: Dense feedback adds value specifically when coupled to skill evolution (C3 to C4 at a matched EA budget).
claims.evidence: Table 3: C3 3/8 (27.0%) versus C4 6/8 (33.6%) at an equal 640 rollouts. This is a fair within-method comparison, but it rests on 8 tasks with no CIs on pass rate; Figure 3 shows only SEM on proxy metrics.

claims.claim: The AgentQ proxy tracks hidden pass/fail closely (r=0.90, AUC 0.982).
claims.evidence: §3.2 and Figure 2, on 96 seed-skill baseline rollouts. This is calibrated on the same OSS24 task pool and not validated on evolved-skill rollouts.

claims.claim: It solves tasks that also defeat frontier agents (Claude Code, Codex).
claims.evidence: Appendix Table 4 marks the tasks. The frontier agents were run once per task in their native harness (Table 2: 12/24 each), so the comparison is a single shot versus 80 tuned rollouts.

patterns.note: Evolved skill text raises solved-task count on the tasks it was tuned on. The authors also report that shared skills transferred unreliably across tasks (§1), which undercuts reuse.
The skill document is treated as an evolvable policy injected per task.
Budgeted dense verifier feedback (at most 3 calls, sanitized) improved outcomes (C1 to C2 0 to 2/8; C3 to C4 3 to 6/8). For NoobsCpu, all 35 passes used feedback (§4.4).
Every stage writes traceability artifacts (§2.3, App. A4).
Per-rollout call budgets and a 30-turn cap are used, but token and dollar cost is never reported despite being acknowledged as compute-intensive (§4.5).

methodology.sample: 24 OSS CVDP tasks for the baseline (6 per CID); 8 hard tasks for the ablation.
methodology.baselines: Seed-skill agent (32 rollouts), Claude Code and Codex in native harnesses (single runs). Compute is not matched against Trace2Skill (640 rollouts).
methodology.models: Claude Opus 4.6 for rollouts, GPT-5 as oracle, Claude Sonnet 4.5 as mutator. Only one rollout model is tested.
methodology.variance: 4 repeats per candidate, with SEM on proxy metrics in Figure 3. No CIs on pass rates.
methodology.contamination_controls: Hidden harnesses and reference solutions are kept from the agent. However, selection uses hidden-verifier outcomes on the same tasks being reported, so test labels feed the optimizer.

standards.artifacts: No code URL. The appendix has trace excerpts and a component map; full traces are 'in the experiment directories' and not released.

biases.detail: Skills are optimized and evaluated on the same 8 tasks, with hidden-verifier outcomes as the leading selection term (§3.1, §3.2).
8 hard tasks; 'solved' can mean 1 pass in 80.
The compute-unmatched baseline (32 vs 640 rollouts) and single-shot frontier agents are compared against best-of-many evolution.
Only Claude Opus 4.6 is used as the rollout agent.
No token, dollar, or wall-clock figures for 640 rollouts per configuration, although the paper admits the method is compute-intensive.
Authors evaluate their own method on a benchmark co-authored by one of them, using their own metrics (AgentQ, SelectQ).

coi.vendor_products_evaluated: CVDP benchmark (Pinckney is first author of the CVDP paper) and NeMo Gym (NVIDIA) as rollout infrastructure. Anthropic and OpenAI models are used as components.
coi.detail: The authors' own method is run on their organization's benchmark and infrastructure and judged by their own proxy metrics. No commercial product is promoted, but there is no independent replication.

verdict_reason: The ablation design (C1-C4) is sensible, and the matched-budget C3 versus C4 comparison is informative. The headline 6/8 is test-time search on the evaluation tasks themselves, with 20x more compute than the baseline, no held-out split, 8 tasks, no cost data, and no code. Treat it as evidence that budgeted verifier feedback helps search, not that evolved skills transfer.
applicability: Mostly does not transfer: Verilog and EDA tasks with per-task skill evolution at about 640 rollouts per configuration are far from Java service work. Two narrow lessons do apply. First, a budgeted, sanitized verifier tool (at most 3 calls, only after an edit and compile) is a reasonable harness design for the team's Java build and contract tests across repositories. Second, the authors report that shared skills transfer poorly across heterogeneous tasks, so a SKILL.md tuned on one repo should not be assumed to help another. Do not adopt per-task skill evolution without cost accounting, and keep evolved skill files under spec review, since they are LLM-written policy.
